title: AI implementation roadmap: what should we do first, and when?
description: Answer nine quick questions. Get a dated AI plan for a 40 to 500 person firm: groundwork, up to 3 projects, owners, review steps and checkpoints.
verdict: Start with two projects, not twenty: AI leaders pursue about half as many opportunities and scale more[^8][^9].
Buy or set up a tool first: bought tools succeed about 67% of the time, twice the internal-build rate[^1][^2].
Write a one-page policy and approve one tool by day 15, since most staff lack AI guidance[^11][^1].
Take a baseline before the pilot; tracking clear measures had the biggest bottom-line effect of any adoption practice[^6][^7].
Judge year one on use, time and errors, because payback on a typical AI use case often takes years[^12][^3].

steps: Pick your industry, your company size and up to three teams to start with.
Tell us how you use AI today, your policy, your data, the stakes and your budget.
Read the plan summary first. Then read each project's owner, review step and gate.
Type in your owners' names and a start date, and every step gets a date.
Copy or print the plan for your team, or bring it to the free diagnostic.
method: Projects come from the AI use case finder's evidence for your industry and teams. Score = finder score × data fit × budget fit, a Zavient method[^4][^18].
Project 1 is a bought or set-up tool with low or medium risk. Bought tools reached daily use about twice as often as internal builds[^1].
Two pilots in the first 90 days only at 100+ people, $25K+ and a named owner. Never more than three projects in year one[^8][^9].
A one-page policy by day 14 and an approved tool by day 15. At least 5 hours of training before anyone uses it on live work[^11][^10].
Each gate says scale, fix or stop, because many AI projects never reach production[^3][^5]. Scale needs 60% weekly use and a measure that beats the baseline, a Zavient threshold you can change.
Review steps follow risk. People approve everything that reaches customers for 60 days, and every decision about people, always[^7][^15].

summary: The AI roadmap builder turns your answers into a dated plan: who owns it, which projects come first, and when to stop. AI drafts, sorts and suggests, while people check and decide[^7][^16]. What makes or breaks it is a baseline and a written review step before the pilot[^6][^15].
humanRole: The COO or owner-CEO sponsors the plan and makes each scale, fix or stop call. Senior ownership of AI work tracks with results[^7][^9].
The head of each team owns its project, such as the head of customer service, the controller or the claims manager[^1][^6].
People send, approve, sign and decide, while AI drafts, sorts and suggests. Firms using AI raised output per worker with no drop in jobs[^16][^17].
Decisions about people's credit, insurance, health or jobs keep a person on every call, with a log and a second check[^7][^15].

ownData.title: What plan does the builder give a 150-person insurance firm?
ownData.intro: We ran the worked example from our research through the builder. Inputs: insurance, 150 people, service, claims and finance teams, personal AI accounts, no policy, messy data, $25K to $100K, and the COO owns it.
rows: Sign a one-page AI use policy by day 14. Approve one AI tool by day 15.
Baselines: issues resolved per agent hour, and days sales outstanding.
Pilot suggested replies with 12 service agents after 5 hours of training.
Pilot collections follow-up. Staff still send every email themselves.
Gate: scale if 8 of 12 agents use it weekly and issues per hour beat the baseline.
Pilot claim letters. A person approves every letter for at least 60 days.
On deck: customer chat for common questions, after its data cleanup.
ownData.note: Zavient worked example, 26 Nov 2026. Scores from the use case finder: suggested replies 85, collections follow-up 47.6, claim letters 44.8. Pilot sizes and gate thresholds are Zavient method judgments.

faq.q: What should an AI roadmap include?
faq.a: Two or three named projects, an owner for each, what comes first, the review step people keep, and dated checkpoints[^6][^7]. High performers are more likely to have a clearly defined AI road map[^7].

faq.q: How long until we see results from AI?
faq.a: Top mid-market firms went from pilot to full use in about 90 days; across firms it averages 8 months from prototype to production[^1][^3]. Payback takes longer, often 2 to 4 years in a survey of European and Middle East firms[^12]. Productivity often dips before it rises[^13][^14].

faq.q: Who should own the AI plan at a company our size?
faq.a: One executive sponsor, usually the COO or owner-CEO, plus the head of each team whose work changes[^9][^1]. Senior leaders who own AI work are far more common at high performers[^7].

faq.q: How many AI projects should we start with?
faq.a: Two in the first 90 days, and no more than three in year one. AI leaders pursue about half as many opportunities and align on three to four priorities[^8][^9].

faq.q: Do we need an AI policy and training before rollout?
faq.a: Yes, and both fit in the first month. Only 40% of employees say their workplace has AI guidance, and 47% have had training[^11]. At least 5 hours of training sharply raises regular use[^10].

faq.q: Do we need clean data before we start with AI?
faq.a: No, but data decides which projects go first. Start with bought tools on documents people already handle, and start one cleanup task early[^4][^18].

faq.q: Should we buy or build our first AI project?
faq.a: Buy or set up first: bought or partner-built tools reached daily use about twice as often as internal builds, in a small self-reported sample[^1].

pickElse: You don't know which work to start with yet: run the AI use case finder first, then come back[^1].
You have one project in mind and need its price: use the AI project cost estimator, then the AI ROI (return on investment) calculator[^3].
Your data sits in paper files and inboxes: take the AI readiness check first, since data gaps stop many projects[^4][^18].

sources.name: MIT NANDA, The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025 (Jul 2025)
sources.what: MIT no longer hosts the report (its link now opens the NANDA project page, checked 26 Nov 2026); copy hosted by MLQ.ai. Sample: 52 organizations interviewed, survey of 153 leaders, and 300+ public AI initiatives reviewed. $30-40 billion of enterprise GenAI investment; 95% of organizations are getting zero return; just 5% of integrated AI pilots extract millions in value. Task-specific tools: 60% of organizations evaluated them, 20% piloted, 5% reached production. Over 80% of organizations explored or piloted ChatGPT or Copilot, and nearly 40% report deployment. External partnerships with customized tools reached deployment about 67% of the time vs about 33% for internal builds: 2x as likely, twice the success rate. Only 40% of companies purchased an official LLM subscription; workers at over 90% of companies surveyed use personal AI tools for work. For mission-critical work, 90% of users prefer humans. Enterprises, defined as firms with over $100 million in annual revenue, lead in pilot count but report the lowest pilot-to-scale conversion. Read 26 Nov 2026.

sources.name: Fortune, MIT report: 95% of generative AI pilots at companies are failing (18 Aug 2025)
sources.what: Fortune's write-up of MIT NANDA's The GenAI Divide report. Headline: 95% of generative AI pilots at companies are failing; about 5% of AI pilot programs achieve rapid revenue acceleration, while the vast majority stall with little to no measurable P&L impact. Purchasing AI tools from specialized vendors and building partnerships succeed about 67% of the time. Its comparison for internal builds misstates the report, where internal builds reach deployment about a third of the time: cite this write-up for the 67% and its headline figures only; MIT's report carries the internal-build rate and the "twice" comparison. Read 28 Nov 2026.

offer.heading: Want a second look at your AI plan before you commit budget? Get a free diagnostic
offer.body: Want the detailed plan behind your result? Book the free 30-minute diagnostic.

reviews.notes: Wanted the plan on one screen with dates. The summary card comes first, the start date sets real dates, and Copy plan and Print give a version to circulate.

Said a 12-person pilot doesn't fit small teams, and a 60-person firm has no IT lead. The pilot now says 'or the whole team if smaller', the gate reads as a share, and IT tasks name an outside IT provider.
Asked what a champion is and why the gate box repeated itself. Champions are defined in the summary and the copied plan; the gate boxes no longer repeat Scale, Fix and Stop.

As head of underwriting, said internal guideline answers never 'leave' the firm. The review step now reads 'before it is sent, posted or acted on', and decisions on people wait until month 4 with a person deciding.
Wanted to know what the free call would settle. The offer names their first project, its owner and the day-14 or day-15 step, and lists what the 30 minutes decides.

answers.human-role: The COO or owner-CEO sponsors the plan and makes each scale, fix or stop call, while each team's head owns its project[^7][^9][^1]. People approve, send and decide; AI only drafts, sorts and suggests[^16].
answers.own-data: A 150-person insurance firm gets a one-page policy and an approved tool by day 15, two pilots by day 46, and a scale-or-stop check at day 90. Claim letters follow in months 4-6, with a person approving every letter.
answers.something-else: Pick something else when you don't yet know which work to start with, already have one project to price, or keep your data in paper files and inboxes[^1][^3][^4]. Start with the AI use case finder, the AI project cost estimator or the AI readiness check instead.
